rows.speaker: الشهاب
rows.claim: Al-Shihab says the Fatiha encompasses two of the three modes of signification: implication and entailment.
rows.anchor: من أن ذلك لإشتمالها على دلالة التضمن والإلتزام وهما ثلثا الدلالات

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Al-Dailami reports from Abu al-Darda that the Fatiha suffices where no other Quran passage does and outweighs the Quran sevenfold on the scales; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: ولو أن فاتحة الكتاب جعلت في كفة الميزان وجعل القرآن في الكفة الأخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the report most naturally promises multiplied reward, which conflicts with the preceding explanation and the view he quotes.
rows.anchor: فأنه لا يتبادر منه إلا الفضل في الثواب فيعارض ظاهره ذلك الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He offers several reconciliations: the reports concern successive stages of reward, differing circumstances, equivalence to two thirds, or Quran understood as prayer.
rows.anchor: ويمكن التوفيق بين الخبرين وبه يزول الإشكال بأن الأول كان أولا وتضاعف الثواب ثانيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconciliation takes Quran in one or both reports to mean prayer, as in this verse; its merit varies with people’s levels of recitation and prayer.
rows.anchor: أو بأن القرآن في أحد الخبرين أو فيهما بمعنى الصلاة مثله في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Reported explanations of the name Fatiha call it the best surah, equal in sanctity to the whole Quran, the refuge of believers, or the mother of the Book as a decisive surah; Al-Alusi says naming reasons need not apply uniformly.
rows.anchor: لأنها أفضل السور أو لأن حرمتها كحرمة القرآن كله أو لأن مفزع أهل الإيمان إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Fatiha gathers the Book’s meanings, its seven absent letters may show that spiritual completeness does not require formal completeness; their number matches its verses, and they are dark letters absent from the ambiguous opening sequences.
rows.anchor: لعل ذلك للإشارة إلى أن الكمال المعنوي لا يلزمه الكمال الصوري ولا ينقصه نقصانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says every luminous letter occurs in the Fatiha while only seven dark letters occur, signifying beauty’s predominance over majesty and the repeated language of mercy.
rows.anchor: وهي النورانية المشتملة عليها بأسرها الفاتحة للإشارة إلى غلبة الجمال على الجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pairing luminous and dark letters symbolizes believers whose faith is unmixed and those whose faith is mixed with sin; this affirms that sin does not erase faith, and yields three classes as in 35:32.
rows.anchor: وإذا طوبقت الآحاد يحصل نوراني معه ظلماني ونوراني خالص إشارة إلى قسمي المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He interprets the dark-only, luminous-only, and mixed forms as the sinful, pure believer, and mixed believer, respectively, linking the scheme to the three classes in 35:32.
rows.anchor: يظهر سر التثليث في ( فمنهم ظالم لنفسه ومنهم مقتصد ومنهم سابق بالخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Why precisely these seven letters were omitted is a secret known to some; their being dotted letters hints at concealment and doubt, an obscure allusion Al-Alusi presents tentatively.
rows.anchor: نعم في كون الساقط معجما فقط إشارة إلى أن الغين في العين والرين في البين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the hints he can discern are slight beside the secrets revealed to mystics immersed in the Quran’s depths.
rows.anchor: وهذا ما يلوح لأمثالنا من أسرار كتاب الله تعالى وأين هو مما يظهر للعارفين الغارقين

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi explains the missing letters as allusions to punishment: thubur, Jahannam, disgrace, infernal sounds, zaqqum, misery, the three-forked shade, laza, and separation; Al-Alusi dismisses this as lacking real investigation.
rows.anchor: ولمولانا العلامة فخر الدين الرازي في هذا المقام كلام ليس له في التحقيق أدنى إلمام

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report attributed to Abu Hurayra likens the heart to a king with troops and the tongue to its interpreter.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي هريرة القلب ملك وله جنود إلى أن قالوا للسان ترجمان الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects the objection that a Christian poet’s hostility makes his wording inadmissible or forces it to be treated metaphorically to protect revelation.
rows.anchor: فما قيل إن هذا الشاعر نصراني عدو الله تعالى ورسوله فيجب أطراح كلام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the poet’s words agree with the beloved’s speech, even with the language of those who deny inner speech while implicitly acknowledging it.
rows.anchor: فلأن كلام هذا العدو موافق لكلام الحبيب حتى لكلام المنكرين للكلام النفسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says Ibn al-Khashshab’s failure to find the poem in old al-Akhtal collections does not prove the verse never existed.
rows.anchor: فقد فتش إبن الخشاب دواوين الأخطل العتيقة فلم يجد فيها البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He portrays the debate over divine speech as subtle and contentious, causing anxiety, controversy, hardship, and imprisonment, and says his own account distilled earlier scholarship.
rows.anchor: البحث دقيق لا يرشد إليه إلا توفيق كم أسهر أناسا وأكثر وسواسا وأثار فتنة

rows.speaker: غنى زاده
rows.claim: Ghani Zada argues that all meanings eternally exist in divine knowledge, while an eternal inner-speech attribute calls for some meanings to appear later in created verbal form; this differs from the attribute of knowledge.
rows.anchor: لما كان في ماهية بعضها داعية البروز في الخارج بوجود لفظي حادث حسبما يستدعيه حدوث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi calls this an audacious invention of an eternal attribute named divine volition or demand: neither Quran, Sunna, Companions, nor Successors name it speech, and reason does not require it.
rows.anchor: وفيه أنه غاية الغايات في الجسارة على رب الأرباب وإحداث صفة قديمة ما أنزل الله تعالى بها من كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says al-Maturidi, al-Ashari, and other investigators hold that Moses actually heard God’s speech in letters and sound, supported by abundant texts that should not be reinterpreted.
rows.anchor: الذي إنتهى إليه كلام أئمة الدين كالماتريدي والأشعري وغيرهما من المحققين أن موسى عليه السلام سمع كلام الله تعالى بحرف وصوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that Quranic descriptions of God calling Moses, together with Arabic usage and hadiths, make a vocal sound the fitting meaning of the divine call.
rows.anchor: واللائق بمقتضى اللغة والأحاديث أن يفسر النداء بالصوت بل قد ورد إثبات الصوت لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi lists rhetoric, hadith, legal theory, theology, and variant readings among the disciplines needed for exegesis: rhetoric explains effects of expression, hadith supplies occasions and abrogation, legal theory handles scope and commands, theology addresses doctrine, and readings resolve possible meanings.
rows.anchor: علم المعاني والبيان والبديع ويعرف بالأول خواص تراكيب الكلام من جهة إفادتها المعنى

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti adds morphology and derivation, which Al-Alusi thinks follow from mastery of the listed sciences; Suyuti includes jurisprudence although other authors omit it.
rows.anchor: وعد السيوطي مما يحتاج إليه المفسر علم التصريف وعلم الإشتقاق وأنا أظن أن المهارة

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti calls divinely bestowed insight a required discipline and cites the report that acting on what one knows brings knowledge of what one did not know.
rows.anchor: من عمل بما علم أورثه الله علم ما لم يعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says inspired knowledge, even if acquired through practice, helps disclose hidden secrets rather than basic Quranic meanings; its recipients often cannot articulate or prove what they receive, so it is interpretation rather than exegesis.
rows.anchor: علم الموهبة بعد تسليم أنه كسبي إنما يحتاج إليه في الإطلاع على الأسرار لا في أصل فهم معاني القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو داود والترمذي والنسائي
rows.claim: The common prohibition on interpretation by personal opinion cites a report that one who comments on the Quran by opinion errs even if correct; Al-Alusi notes that its soundness is disputed.
rows.anchor: من تكلم في القرآن برأيه فأصاب فقد أخطأ وفي رواية عن أبي داؤد

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة
rows.claim: Most authorities say the Fatiha is Meccan, among the earliest revelations; this is reported from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and most Companions.
rows.anchor: وهو المروى عن علي وإبن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the Fatiha is Medinan; he is said to have been alone in this view, which was counted as a mistake.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنها مدنية وقد تفرد بذلك حتى عد هفوة منه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says it descended in Mecca when prayer became obligatory and again in Medina when the qibla changed, affirming its continued place in prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل نزلت بمكة حين فرضت الصلاة وبالمدينة لما حولت القبلة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view that some of the Fatiha is Meccan and some Medinan is weak, in Al-Alusi’s judgment.
rows.anchor: وقيل بعضها مكي وبعضها مدني ولا يخفى ضعفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan case appeals to 15:87, which scholars and Ibn Abbas identify as referring to the seven oft-repeated verses; however, Ibn Abbas and others also interpret these as the seven long surahs.
rows.anchor: على مكيتها بآية الحجر ( ولقد آتيناك سبعا من المثاني والقرآن العظيم ) وهي مكية لنص العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers Companion testimony from eyewitnesses to revelation as the strongest evidence, since the Meccan argument depends on interpreting the seven oft-repeated verses as the Fatiha.
rows.anchor: والأقوى الإستدلال بالنقل عن الصحابة الذين شاهدوا الوحي التنزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that God cannot promise a gift before its delivery is weakened by Quranic past tense used for a future certainty, as in 48:1, although the emphatic wording and the link to 20:131 suggest prior occurrence.
rows.anchor: وهذا وإن كان خلاف الظاهر لا سيما مع إيراد اللام وكلمة ( قد ) ووروده في معرض المنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects repeated descent: revelation is a manifestation from the unseen to the visible and cannot recur; claims of different benefits, readings, or presence of the basmala do not prove a second descent, and reports merely establish occurrence rather than cause it.
rows.anchor: والظهور بها لا يقبل التكرر فإن ظهور الظاهر ظاهر البطلان كتحصيل الحاصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surah may derive from sur, a remnant, or from the enclosing wall of a building; it may also derive from elevation, as in al-Nabigha’s line where sura means rank or eminence.
rows.anchor: ألم تر أن الله أعطاك سورة ترى كل ملك حولها يتذبذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A surah is an independent Quranic unit with an opening and conclusion; the alternative definition as a self-contained section would require Ayat al-Kursi’s surah status to be established by transmitted designation. Surah names are established by reports.
rows.anchor: وحدها قرآن يشتمل على ذي فاتحة وخاتمة وقيل طائفة مستقلة لتخرج آية الكرسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi dismisses the prohibition on saying Sura X: Anas’s report is weak or fabricated, while Ibn Umar’s is authentic in chain but only his own statement.
rows.anchor: إذ حديث أنس ضعيف أو موضوع وحديث ابن عمر موقوف عليه وإن روى عنه بسند صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatiha is grammatically a descriptive noun for the first part that opens the whole; it may be a transferred adjective or a verbal noun used for its object, while instrumental and causal derivations are less apt and a relational derivation is possible but weaker.
rows.anchor: والفاتحة ) في الأصل صفة جعلت إما لأول الشيء لكونه واسطة في فتح الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the Kitab is the concrete whole, so Fatiha is first relative to this particular compilation, which exists in divine knowledge, the Preserved Tablet, or Bayt al-Izza; the first genitive is name-to-named and the second means of, not from.
rows.anchor: والكتاب ( هو المجموع الشخصي وفتح الفاتحة بالقياس إليه لا إلى القدر المشترك

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari reports that God gathers people and calls in a voice heard equally by those far away and those near: I am the King, the Judge.
rows.anchor: يحشر الله العباد فيناديهم بصوت يسمعه من بعدكما يسمعه من قرب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the blessed one in the fire as God Himself: the Lord of the worlds’ light was in the tree; another report says God was in the light and called from it.
rows.anchor: يعني تبارك وتعالى نفسه كان نور رب العالمين في الشجرة وفي رواية عنه

rows.speaker: مسلم
rows.claim: Muslim transmits two descriptions of God’s veil: it is light in one report and fire in another.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم حجابه النور وفي رواية له حجابه النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For mystics, God can disclose Himself as He wills without being confined by appearances; His absolute transcendence remains even in manifestation, resolving difficulties about divine appearance in a form.
rows.anchor: وأنه منزه في تجليه قريب في تعاليه لا تقيده المظاهر عند أرباب الأذواق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi reads the glorification as denying that God is confined to the image, location, or direction from which He calls; manifestation does not limit the Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: أي عن التقييد بالصورة والمكان والجهة وإن ناداك منها لكونه موصوفا بصفة رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains that divine might precludes limitation while divine wisdom calls for disclosure in the requested fire-form; Moses therefore heard God’s letters and sound directly, behind the fire’s veil, through divine light manifested there.
rows.anchor: فالمسموع على هذا صوت وحرف سمعهما موسى عليه السلام من الله تعالى المتجلي بنوره في مظهر النار

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the common attribution to al-Ashari that Moses actually heard inner speech is mistaken; al-Ashari allowed such hearing as a possibility, not what occurred.
rows.anchor: وأما ما شاع عن الأشعري من القول بسماع الكلام النفسي القائم بذات الله تعالى فهو من باب التجويز والإمكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sacred hadith about God becoming a beloved servant’s hearing shows how, through luminous self-disclosure, the servant may extraordinarily hear nonmaterial speech while remaining within the principle of 42:11.
rows.anchor: كنت سمعه الذي يسمع به الحديث ومن الواضح أن الله تبارك وتعالى إذا كان بتجليه النوري

rows.speaker: الماتريدي
rows.claim: Al-Maturidi also permits extraordinary hearing of what is not sound, according to al-Tabṣira; Ibn al-Humam’s report of impossibility refers only to ordinary impossibility, so there is no substantive disagreement between the two imams.
rows.anchor: والإمام الماتريدي أيضا يجوز سماع ما ليس بصوت على وجه خرق العادة

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Alusi explains that during recitation what is directly heard is the reciter’s verbal speech; its letters are forms of God’s hidden essential speech, which is thereby heard through the form and only heard directly by supernatural means.
rows.anchor: المسموع أو لا وبالذات عند التلاوة إنما هو الكلام اللفظي الذي حروفه عارضة لصوت القاريء

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani’s claim that one hears recitation rather than what is recited can mean only that the verbal utterance is heard directly, leaving no real disagreement on Al-Alusi’s reading.
rows.anchor: إنما تسمع التلاوة دون المتلو والقراءة دون المقروء يمكن حمله على أنه أراد

rows.speaker: الطبرسي
rows.claim: Al-Tabrisi says adding to the Quran is universally rejected, while some Imamis and some Sunni traditionalists alleged omission; he says al-Murtada defended the correct denial of omission.
rows.anchor: أما الزيادة فيه أي القرآن فمجمع على بطلانها وأما النقصان فقد روى عن قوم من أصحابنا

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtada argues that reliable transmission of the Quran is as certain as knowledge of countries, major events, famous books, and recorded Arabic poetry, with still stronger motives to preserve it because it grounds prophecy and religious law.
rows.anchor: وذكر في مواضع أن العلم بصحة نقل القرآن كالعلم بالبلدان والحوادث الكبار والوقائع العظام

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: He argues that Muslim scholars precisely tracked every difference in parsing, reading, letters, and verses, making alteration or loss implausible under their strong care and control.
rows.anchor: وعلماء المسلمين قد بلغوا في حفظه وحمايته الغاية حتى عرفوا كل شيء أختلف فيه من إعرابه وقراءته

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Knowledge of the Quran’s detailed parts is as certain as knowledge of the whole, like specialists’ knowledge of Sibawayh’s and al-Muzani’s books; an insertion would be detected, and care for Quran transmission was greater still.
rows.anchor: أن العلم بتفصيل القرآن وأبعاضه في صحة نقله كالعلم بجملته

rows.speaker: المرتضى
rows.claim: Al-Murtada says the Quran was fully compiled and ordered in the Prophet’s lifetime: it was studied, memorized, recited to him, and repeatedly completed by Companions such as Ibn Masud and Ubayy.
rows.anchor: وأن جماعة من الصحابة مثل عبدالله بن مسعود وأبي بن كعب وغيرهما ختموا القرآن على النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم عدة ختمات

rows.speaker: الطبرسي
rows.claim: Al-Tabrisi dismisses dissenting Imamis and traditionalists as not authoritative because they relied on weak reports they mistakenly considered sound, which cannot outweigh certain knowledge.
rows.anchor: لا يعتد بخلافهم فإن الخلاف في ذلك مضاف إلى قوم من أصحاب الحديث نقلوا أخبارا ضعيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says al-Tabrisi’s defense of Quranic integrity mixes falsehood into truth and falsely attributes an omission doctrine to Sunni traditionalists.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الرجل قد دس في الشهد سما وأدخل الباطل في حمى الحق الأحمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says Sunnis unanimously deny loss of any mass-transmitted Quranic text now between the covers; reports of omitted material refer instead to non-mutawatir readings, abrogated recitation, or material not present in the final review.
rows.anchor: لأنهم أجمعوا على قدم وقوع النقص فيما تواترا قرآنا كما هو موجود بين الدفتين اليوم

words: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَمَلَٰٓئِكَتَهُۥ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِىِّ
rows.speaker: حميدة بنت يونس
rows.claim: Humayda bint Yunus reports that Aisha’s codex included this verse followed by a phrase about those who pray in the first rows, before Uthman changed the codices; the excerpt gives no grading.
rows.anchor: كما روى عن حميدة بنت يونس أن في مصحف عائشة رضي الله عنها

rows.speaker: المدخل
rows.claim: Al-Madkhal says the first opinion-based exegesis report, if authentic, condemns bypassing the proper sources: return word meanings to linguists, abrogation to reports, and intended meaning to the Prophet; where these offer no answer, evidence-based reasoning is allowed.
rows.anchor: الطريق الرجوع في تفسير ألفاظه إلى أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: المدخل
rows.claim: Alternatively, the warning targets those who make their doctrine or desire primary and force the Quran to support it; the preposition in the report then denotes causal opinion.
rows.anchor: أو أراد من قال بالقرآن قولا يوافق هواه بأن يجعل المذهب أصلا والتفسير تابعا له

rows.speaker: المدخل
rows.claim: The warning may concern ambiguous passages whose meaning God alone knows, or asserting God’s intended meaning categorically without proof.
rows.anchor: أو يقال ذلك في المتشابه الذي لا يعلمه إلا الله أو في الجزم بأن مراد الله تعالى كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second hadith can mean that one who speaks without knowledge about a difficult Quranic question risks divine anger, or that one who knowingly states a false interpretation faces the Fire.
rows.anchor: وأما الحديث الثاني فله معنيان الأول من قال في مشكل القرآن بما لا يعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says Quranic commands to refer questions to qualified investigators and to ponder the text support reasoned exegesis, citing 4:83, 47:24, and 38:29.
rows.anchor: ولو ردوه إلى الرسول وإلى أولي الأمر منهم لعلمه الذين يستنبطونه منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites Ibn Abbas’s report that the Quran is pliable and multivalent and should be read in its best sense, the Prophet’s prayer that Ibn Abbas learn religion and interpretation, and Ali’s denial that the Prophet gave the family hidden scripture beyond the written text and understanding.
rows.anchor: القرآن ذلول ذو وجوه فأحملوه على أحسن وجوهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects the claim that understanding Quranic constructions depends entirely on transmitted exegesis, since commentators differ widely and Prophetic explanations of such meanings are exceptionally rare.
rows.anchor: والعجب كل العجب مما يزعم أن علم التفسير مضطر إلى النقل في فهم معاني التراكيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qualified interpretation belongs to someone deeply versed in Arabic, spiritual discernment, and religious sciences, who recognizes Quranic inimitability directly and can reach its deeper meanings.
rows.anchor: من كان متبحرا في علم اللسان مترقيا منه إلى ذوق العرفان وله في رياض العلوم الدينية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those absorbed in Aristotelian speculations and preferring thorns to peacock feathers cannot grasp the Quran’s subtleties and wonders.
rows.anchor: وأما من صرف عمره بوساوس أرسطاطاليس وأختار شوك القنافذ على ريش الطواويس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi readings disclose subtle allusions to practitioners and can accord with the intended outward meanings; they do not replace the apparent sense with a hidden one, a doctrine Al-Alusi attributes to esoteric heretics who seek to abolish the law.
rows.anchor: يمكن التطبيق بينها وبين الظواهر المرادة وذلك من كمال الإيمان ومحض العرفان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says Sufi masters themselves urged preservation of the outward exegesis.
rows.anchor: كيف وقد حضوا على حفظ التفسير الظاهر
